Posted June 11, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: On May 24th the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued an adverse ruling on the long standing suit by former NORML National Director, Jon Gettman, and High Times magazine.

Gettman was simply seeking to force the DEA to agree to the rescheduling of cannabis from Schedule I to Schedule II, so that it could be prescribed by doctors.

Marijuana does not really belong in Schedule II, of course, but this is the starting point.

However, the court did not rule on the merits of the case, but simply said that Gettman was not a patient, was not an injured party, and therefore lacked " standing " to bring the suit. The ruling is on line at http://laws.lp.findlaw.com/dc/011182.html

Consequently, the case is going to be refiled with patients as the plaintiffs. Gettman began working on his response to the Court's ruling the day after the hearing.

However, that is not how the DEA chose to tell the story.

Also note that although the ruling was on May 24th, they waited until June 6th, the day of the national protests against the federal suppression of medical cannabis to issue a press release, and then they lied about it.

They were wasting their time. It got even less coverage than the protests.)

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

From the DEA web site at

June 6, 2002

HIGH COURT UPHOLDS MARIJUANA AS DANGEROUS DRUG

The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued a ruling on May 24, 2002, upholding DEA's determination that marijuana must remain a schedule I controlled substance. The Court of Appeals rejected an appeal filed by High Times Magazine and Jon Gettman, who contended that marijuana does not meet the legal criteria for classification in schedule I, the most restrictive schedule under the Controlled Substances Act.

DEA Director Asa Hutchinson stated: " This is an important ruling because it leaves in place a sound decision made by DEA, in consultation with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), that there is no basis to remove marijuana from schedule I. Current medical and scientific evidence continues to demonstrate that marijuana has a high potential for abuse and no safe and effective medical use. "

Mr. Gettman petitioned DEA in 1995 to remove marijuana from schedule I. Under the Controlled Substances Act, schedule I substances must meet three strict criteria. These substance must have: no accepted medical use in treatment in the United States, a lack of accepted safety for use under medical supervision, and a high potential for abuse. Mr. Gettman and High Times Magazine sought through their petition to move marijuana to a schedule where it may be prescribed by physicians for medical use.

Director Hutchinson explained the importance of accurate drug scheduling: " Drugs sold lawfully in the United States are the safest in the world.This is because our nation, through its laws, insists on careful deliberation before allowing drugs to be sold as medicine. To date, marijuana does not meet the scientific requirements. "

In accordance with Federal law, DEA referred the petition to the HHS for a scientific and medical evaluation. After conducting an extensive evaluation, the FDA advised DEA that current scientific and medical evidence demonstrates that marijuana continues to meet all three statutory criteria for placement in schedule I.

DEA agreed with the HHS's conclusions and denied the petition to reschedule marijuana saying that the evidence overwhelmingly leads to the conclusion that marijuana has a high potential for abuse. DEA's denial of the petition, along with the complete details of the medical and scientific findings made by DEA and the HHS, were published April 18, 2001, in the Federal Register (volume 66, page 20038).

Following DEA's denial of their petition, Mr. Gettman and High Times Magazine appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The D.C. Circuit rejected the appeal on May 24, 2002, holding that Mr. Gettman and High Times Magazine lack standing to appeal under the United States Constitution. The Court's ruling lets stand DEA's denial of the petition to reschedule marijuana.

(MarijuanaNews note: They lie in the headline and all the way through the press release, then tell the real reason in the last paragraph.

What makes this all the more dishonest is the fact that whether or not marijuana is a " dangerous drug " has no relevance to whether it should be in Schedule I or Schedule II, because both categories are for drugs with a " high potential for abuse. "

The only difference between the Schedules is whether there is an " accepted medical use. " The court did not rule on that at all.

DEA Director Hutchinson is a former US Attorney from Arkansas and knows perfectly well what this ruling meant. But he also knows that he was hired to suppress the truth about many things.)
